chunks: I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about cotton and saffron: 'Is there zakat upon them?' He said: 'No.'

key_terms.الزَّعْفَرَانِ: Saffron (al-za'faran) — a prized spice derived from the Crocus sativus flower; used medicinally, in food, and in dye; historically valuable as a trade commodity
key_terms.الْقُطْنِ: Cotton (al-qutn) — a fiber crop cultivated widely in the Islamic world for textile production; not a food staple
key_terms.زَكَاةٌ: Zakat — obligatory alms-tax, one of the five pillars of Islam; in Shia jurisprudence, agricultural zakat applies to specific crops only

ai.seo_question: Is there zakat on cotton and saffron in Islam?
ai.summary: In this brief legal ruling, Imam al-Ridha (peace be upon him) is asked by Abd al-Aziz ibn al-Muhtadi whether zakat is obligatory on cotton and saffron — two agricultural commodities valued in the Islamic world. The Imam's concise answer, 'No,' establishes that these two crops are not among the items subject to zakat. Classical Islamic jurisprudence generally limits obligatory zakat on crops to the four grains and staples (wheat, barley, dates, and raisins), and this hadith confirms that non-food or non-staple crops like cotton and saffron are exempt.
